passage:
Day one: at their Ranchi flat, Leela, five, shouted "I want juice!" across the hall. Her mother Seema said, "Indoor voice, please, Leela," and she whispered, "I want juice." Seema said, "Thank you, well tried."
Day three: Leela shouted again but caught herself. "Sorry, indoor voice. Juice, please."
Day six: at the playground she screamed with joy on the slide, and Seema said, "That's your outdoor voice, perfect." At home, they made a small picture card with a mouth.

qa.q: What did Leela shout on day one?
qa.a: She shouted, "I want juice!" across the hall.

qa.q: What might Leela have been feeling when she caught herself on day three?
qa.a: She probably wanted juice and got excited, then remembered the reminder and wanted to show she could do it. Her "Sorry" suggests she knew the rule.

qa.q: What helped Leela learn to swap a yell for an indoor voice?
qa.a: Clear reminders, praise for trying and a shared picture card gave her a signal she could use.

qa.q: How might Seema feel as Leela gets better at this?
qa.a: She may feel pleased and patient, since the change is gradual and the card helps both of them.

grounding: A child learns to swap a yell for an indoor voice, and clear rules, praise and a shared signal help self-control grow.

passage: The heavy traffic outside the Toronto clinic drowned out every sound, and Tobias, five, screamed "Hamid, look, a helicopter!" at his uncle, standing right beside him. Hamid smiled and touched his ear. "Here, outdoors, that voice is fine." He took out a small card with a finger-on-lips drawing. "Inside the clinic, use the quiet one." Inside, Tobias remembered, pointed at the card his uncle had shown him, and whispered, "Shh voice." "Well done," whispered Hamid. When the nurse called them, Tobias held the card up to show her.

qa.q: What did Tobias see outside the clinic?
qa.a: He saw a helicopter.

qa.q: What was Tobias feeling when he screamed about the helicopter?
qa.a: He was excited and wanted to share it. The traffic was loud, so he may also have thought he needed to shout to be heard.

qa.q: What could Hamid do to help Tobias use the right voice in future?
qa.a: He can keep using the card and a friendly reminder, and praise Tobias whenever he tries.

qa.q: How might the nurse see Tobias holding up the card?
qa.a: The nurse might find it charming and understand that Tobias is learning to control his voice.

grounding: A child learns to swap a yell for an indoor voice, and a shared signal and praise help.

passage: “MUMMY! LOOK AT MY ROCKET!” Mohit yelled from the balcony to the kitchen. Chandrika came out. She made their signal: turning an invisible knob down with her fingers. Mohit giggled and lowered his voice. “Look at my rocket.” “Much better,” said Chandrika. “Thank you for trying.” She admired the rocket. “Outside at the park, you can be loud. Inside we use this voice.” Mohit nodded. Two minutes later he shouted again, saw her hand turning the knob, and whispered, “Sorry. Rocket's going up.”

qa.q: What signal did Chandrika make?
qa.a: Turning an invisible knob down with her fingers.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he whispered “Sorry. Rocket's going up”?
qa.a: He felt a little sheepish for forgetting again but still excited about his rocket.

qa.q: What helped Mohit learn his indoor voice?
qa.a: A shared signal, a clear rule about inside and outside voices, and praise for trying.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Mohit's second shout?
qa.a: She likely sees it as normal forgetting while learning, not naughtiness, since self-control grows gradually.

grounding: A child learns to swap his yell for an indoor voice with a shared signal, a clear rule and praise.

passage:
“AAAAAH!” Sahil screamed in the hallway.
Asif ran out to his son. “What happened? Are you hurt?”
“No, I'm a dinosaur!”
Asif breathed out. “Phew. You scared me. Screams are for fun outside, or for real danger. Inside, if you scream, I think you're hurt.”
“But dinosaurs roar!”
“Inside dinosaurs roar like this.” Asif did a tiny “rarr.”
Sahil giggled. “Rarr.”
“Perfect. Tomorrow at the park you can roar as big as you like.”
“The biggest roar ever?”
“Deal.”

qa.q: What was Sahil pretending to be?
qa.a: A dinosaur.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he ran out?
qa.a: He was frightened that Sahil was hurt, which is why he breathed out in relief when he heard it was a game.

qa.q: How did Asif explain when screaming is okay?
qa.a: He said screams are for fun outside or for real danger, because inside a scream makes him think someone is hurt.

qa.q: How might Sahil see the rule after the tiny “rarr”?
qa.a: He sees it as fun, not a punishment, and looks forward to the biggest roar at the park.

grounding: A child learns to scream only for fun outside or for danger, and to use a small indoor voice, through a clear rule.

passage:
Note by Elizabeth, KG teacher.
Suraj has a big voice, and in class he often shouts his answers. We started a signal: when I put my hand on my head, it means indoor voice. The first day he forgot six times. Today he forgot only twice, and both times he saw my hand and dropped his voice straight away. I told him, “I saw you trying. That's great.” He beamed. At outdoor play I said, “Now you can shout,” and he shouted “YAAAY!” across the field.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's hand on the head mean?
qa.a: Indoor voice.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when Elizabeth praised him?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, and his beam showed that being noticed for trying mattered to him.

qa.q: Why was praising the trying a good idea?
qa.a: It encourages Suraj to keep working on his voice, since self-control grows gradually.

qa.q: How might the other children see Suraj's shout at outdoor play?
qa.a: They'd see it as normal fun outside, and might join in with their own shouts.

grounding: The note shows a child learning to swap shouting for an indoor voice with a shared signal and praise for trying.

passage:
At the anganwadi in the small town, Rehana yelled "I WANT THE RED BLOCKS!" across the room.

Dolma Teacher put one hand flat on top of her head, their signal. Rehana saw it, put her own hand on her head and said, much more quietly, "I want the red blocks, please."

"That's a lovely indoor voice. Thank you for trying," Dolma Teacher said, and handed them over.

At playtime in the field, Rehana screamed happily while being chased. Dolma Teacher only smiled. Outside, screaming for fun was fine.

qa.q: What was the signal Dolma Teacher used?
qa.a: She put one hand flat on top of her head.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she yelled for the red blocks?
qa.a: She was probably eager and a bit impatient to get the blocks. Copying the signal shows she wanted to get it right once reminded, and she likely felt pleased at the praise.

qa.q: What small step helped Rehana switch to an indoor voice?
qa.a: The shared hand-on-head signal reminded her without a scolding, and praise for trying made her want to do it again. 👍

qa.q: How does Dolma Teacher see Rehana's screaming in the field?
qa.a: She sees it as fine and just smiles, because outside, screaming for fun is allowed.

grounding: It shows a child swapping a yell for an indoor voice when reminded with a shared signal and praise, while screaming for fun outside.
